title: “Cool” Clothes?
content: Where are we shopping for cool/trendy clothes that won’t cost half my paycheck? Especially for kids that are in bigger sizes than their peers! My oldest SS is 9 and in men’s sizes looking to get some clothes for back to school and I’m at a loss! I’ve been hitting the thrift stores looking for Nike/Underarmour/Adidas, all the athletic wear brands. I’ve gotten him a couple character shirts (mainly fortnite as that’s what he likes) but it’s tough to find anything in men’s for a kid that young! What brands are cool now? Please help, I feel so out of touch!

comments.body:
This is a great age to guide your children to pick out their own clothing. They are starting to look around and know what other kids are wearing. 

Going to school? Mostly a free for all, with some exceptions (most schools have some restrictions).  Let them pick out what they love. Ask questions about items you think might look good. You might get a response on why that item isn’t as cool as you think it is. 

Going to Church/dinner out at a restaurant?  Explain why everyone needs a go-to button up, polo, and chino pants. Proper clothes for the proper occasion. 

Set a budget and see if they can stick to it.  Give them the cash and a list of items they need (3 shirts, 2 shorts, jeans). At this age, they are growing quickly, so it’s important to have them try on their clothing in store. They are also at the age where they probably don’t want you in the dressing room with them so let them have their space. 

We usually find a good selection at Gap and Old Navy, and shop their sales heavily.  Our kids are younger, but we frequently let them pick out one shirt/dress if they are with us. 

And finally, although you retain veto privileges, try to be flexible.  I have a visceral disdain for Crocs yet my son really wanted a pair. I allowed it and they are now his go-to pair. Turns out his best friend had a pair and now they match at summer camp.

replies.body:
My step son would rather play video games than go shopping with me lol and we only see them every other weekend so we try to do fun stuff! I do plan on having him try everything on before we send it home to his mom’s and making sure he likes what I ordered and will return anything he doesn’t like! 

I also love the old navy sales and go there often to get clothes for all 3 kids! 

Thank you for the advice :)

Yup. Don't micromanage things like color, my dad did this and to this day I don't understand why he cared so much lol. Huge power struggles if you wanted a color that wasn't primary. 

See what they find within the budget; it might mean they splurge on one item you think is silly, and learn that it means going thriftier on the rest of the items, and be A-OK with that trade-off!

title: 5 year old won’t wear clothes (going on 6 days in a row )
content:
We have a 5 year old and 2.5 year old. As of 6 days ago the 5 year old has stopped wearing clothes - yesterday she has also stopped wearing underwear. 

She says that anything she wears is “too tight” and has a major meltdown. We are at the ends of our sanity. By major meltdown we are talking an hour+ tantrum, running screaming hitting things. She will strip off all articles of clothing. 

She indicates that she does really want to go places and looks forward to it but cannot try any clothes on without shifting into a tantrum. 

She does have a minor history with sensory issues and has called things “too tight” before but this has usually been a preference indicator where she will choose another article for clothing. She is otherwise social and intelligent, and hasn’t ever done this before. She attended preschool. 

She says that she is “figuring it out” and that she needs “many days” to figure out clothes. She often talks about the fun things she will do when she is ready for clothes again. Her appetite, diet, sleep, and everything else behavior wise is completely normal. 

We have tried 
-reinforcing the need for wearing clothes (we can’t go anywhere since people need clothes for that)

-incentivizing special circumstances (if we put our clothes on we can go to a toy store or to grandmas house)

-changing the situation (getting dressed outside or in the car, mid-action) 

-having everyone else get dressed together 

-play dress up games and be silly about dressing with little pressure 

-making being around the house very boring and unengaging, up to and including not doing things because those things are for people with clothes (she waits it out) 

-having clothed friends (largely cousins) over for social situations 

-taking a few day break where we don’t talk about clothes or getting dressed at all

-introducing non-clothing ways for her body to feel pressure and texture (brushing, blankets, etc as a part of other activities or while she is distracted)

-slipping a dress on her at night while she is sleeping

-introducing this as a conversation with her and asking for her advice on what we can do to help her

-frankly, in the first couple of days, attempting to get a dress on and get her into the car (massive tantrum) 

Over the last few days, we 
-talked to her occupational therapist 

-talked to a occupational therapist specializing in sensory issues 

-talked to an emergency pediatric psychologist 

It seems that what amounts to clinical or therapist consensus is to largely take all pressure to get clothes on away and encourage pressure/touch therapy and play with clothes. They suggest that hopefully this warms her up and that she has some sort of anxiety driving this. The clothing specialist said to take all pressure off for 3-5 days, keep her activities and routine as normal as possible  and see what happens. 

Being stuck not being able to go anywhere and feeling completely defeated. I don’t know how we keep a routine normal without going anywhere. Her and the 2.5 butt heads throughout the day. We are feeling like we are stuck in a hellish time loop. Our mental health is taking a nosedive. We do try to limit the amount of exposure our daughters have to this wearing on us (taking breaks, taking turns) but that also has it limits over a week. 

Does anyone have any experience with something like this or anything else to try that isn’t “wait and see” - end of wits and trying to stay supportive as I have to go back to work

comments.body:
Hey, first of all, you’re doing a great job. You’re doing a really, really hard job, and you’re doing well. You’re talking to professionals and to your child and to your partner, and your daughter is going to make it out of this phase okay.

The only suggestion I really have for you is to maybe get her a soft robe to wear around the house. Fleecy, if she likes that texture, or satin or cotton- whatever texture she likes in a blanket/ sheets. I also googled “autism underwear” to find some sensory-friendly underwear, and I found some boy short style underwear that might feel better to her. Maybe her undies ride up, and that bothers her… no idea.

You’ve got this! Keep taking breaks, and keep looking for answers.

title: School clothing style
content:
When you are purchasing your child’s school clothes do you keep a theme in mind? Or do you just buy whatever you find?

My son will hopefully start preschool on August so I want to take advantage of the sales and buy his school clothes, but I don’t know how to dress him. He’s always been home and when we have appointments he gets dressed in the nice clothes. But if he’s just at home he’s in comfy clothes like jersey pants and short sleeve shirts. So would it be better for him to be sent to school in comfortable or in presentable clothing?

comments.body:
I always kept it very basic for school and sort of created our own uniform. I have lived in both warm climates (mostly warm all year) and colder climates (traditional heavy, freezing winter w/ snow & ice). 

For the warmer seasons: Basic shorts in blue, khaki, and brown or grey (b/c black is too hot). I try to have 6-8 pairs of shorts. That way we can get through a week of school without having to wash and then have at least 1 extra to send to school for an emergency, with potentially a few extra pairs in case I forgot to do laundry or something happens and you just run through everything. If you see a mostly clean pair one day, I'm happy to "air and wear" after a day, but for most of elementary school this isn't an option at all.  Then for shirts I do about 8-10 [short sleeved] b/c they tend to gather stains and rips faster. I try to make sure I choose colors that will go with any of the shorts or at least half of the shorts. I also will generally buy at least 1 white t-shirt (b/c they always end up doing an event at some point and ask kids to wear a white t-shirt). And I buy 2 school shirts. One for spirit day, one for pictures or fieldtrips. I do keep a stain stick by the front door so when kids come in from school I can stain-stick them immediately and toss shirts into the laundry. [Also I make my kids change out of school clothes after getting home so they don't get dinner on them or get them messy during after-school playtime.]

For winter, I grab about 6 long-sleeve t-shirts to put under regular t-shirts to keep kids warmer. And for even our warmer climate this is all we use most of the winter to keep warm. I have girls so my go-to was leggings and sweat pants b/c leggings are cheaper than jeans. I'd put the leggings on & they could cover with sweat pants. For boys I assume you could still choose sweat pants but also use jeans. In my warmer climate I only buy about 4 pairs of leggings w/ 2 pairs of sweat pants but in colder climates I used 6-8 pairs of leggings and 6 sweats. At the time the hanes matching tops & bottoms - I would actually buy several sets for school and play. 

I buy my kids 2-3 hoodies for cooler weather now & air them out between uses, but still wash every week/every other week. They also all have 1-2 flannel shirts. In the colder climate I had 2 "nice" winter coats - one to wear, one to air, so that if they came home damp I could let it dry out a full day. Also a fan of the snow bibs, so I usually had a few pairs of those b/c they went outside even when it had snowed. 

Two pairs of regular shoes - so if they got wet or yucky they could be cleaned off & left to air while they wore another pair. And 1 pair of snow boots - and I did buy a size up most years so they could use them all winter, and I did buy a NICE pair so they stayed dry on the inside. 

I always kept it basic. Shorts, leggings/sweatpants or jeans, t-shirts, hanes sweatshirts.

replies.body: Yes! I also wanted to create a uniform of his own. To me that’s a t-shirt and jeans. We live in a snow free area so it usually just rains or gets very cold in the winter. Your quantities are so helpful and smart.

title: Whoa... senior photo time already!??!? (allow me to vent and pick your collective brains)
content:
Senior (yearbook) photos are asking for "Black Own Clothing" for the photo shoot. The reference photos they sent have the boys in a black suit and tie. (Girls are in nice formal dresses)

So we went to two different stores to buy him a suit that he will probably only wear once in his life for a 6-minute photo session. He's not gonna go to senior prom (trust me on this). If he ever has a job interview for an internship or something in college, he would be overdressed for his field of study. If we went to a family wedding (not looking likely for several years), he would wear our cultural dress. By the time he's in the age range to need a suit, he will hopefully have filled out a bit.  
  
He's skinny. Like, in the 1st percentile for his height skinny. The closest size dress pants that would fit him would be 28X32, and would still need to be taken in. They happened to have a size 35 jacket that would not need to be altered, but it was around $200!

His entire wardrobe consists of plain t-shirts and casual pants. Why pretend he's the type of kid who owns a suit? (The sales guy at Men's Warehouse was amazed we were buying a suit just for a yearbook photo).

I'm thinking about having him wear "business casual" with a black dress shirt and pants and a contrasting tie. Would he look completely out of place? I'm guessing it would be easier to find clothing that actually fits and he could wear again.

comments.body: Never heard of a school dictating the outfit of students for their picture. Why can't he wear what he already owns or wants to wear? What are they gonna do?

replies.body:
It's not the school it's the photo studio that does the yearbook pics. They give options for multiple poses: casual clothes with props, cap-and-gown, and the official yearbook photo, which is "Black Own Clothing". He doesn't want to do the casual or cap-and-gown options.

He's allowed to wear whatever he wants, I suppose, as long as it's black. The example photos for the yearbook pics just threw me because they were all in formalwear. Maybe he could just do a Steve Jobs and wear a black turtleneck and black jeans or something?

title: Hoodies in the middle of summer
content:
Anyone else have teen boys who insist on wearing hoodies and joggers when it's 90+ degrees outside? 

Note: This doesn't have to do with covering up self-harm or anything else dangerous. My foster son is fine with t-shirts and shorts in the house but outside he insists on wearing a hoodie and joggers to show off the brand. I took him to a Juneteenth festival today, 93 degrees, he insisted on wearing this. Meanwhile I'm in shorts and a lightweight top and am still sweating. Saw several boys there also in hoodies and joggers. In fact I saw more boys in hoodies than actual summer clothes. I'm also a teacher and every year the amount of boys insisting on wearing this seems to increase. I'm just wondering, is this just a thing with boys in my area or is it a thing parents in other area experience with their boys?

comments.body: The same boys will wear shorts when it’s 20 degrees here.
